newsitem.title: USA: Oppenheimer sees strong aluminum through 1998.
newsitem.headline: Oppenheimer sees strong aluminum through 1998.

text.p: Falling inventories, an end to consumer destocking, and limited upside production potential are combining to paint a healthy picture for aluminum and shares of leading North American producers, brokerage Oppenheimer & Co Inc said in an aluminum report.
"Conditions are ripe to change the global destocking environment into one of restocking before year-end," Oppenheimer said.
The visible catalyst to restocking would have to be a sustained drop in LME stocks. Demand has started to rise again, the brokerage company said.
Reported inventories -- International Primary Aluminium Institute and LME -- should fall 300,000 tonnes in 1997 and by 500,000 tonnes in 1998.
Oppenheimer forecast that aluminum production is set to rise 5 percent in 1997 and 5.4 percent in 1998.

Current production rate for the industry was 93 percent, and it has never operated at 100 percent. Of the remaining 1.19 million tonnes of idled capacity, Alcoa controls 35 percent, Reynolds Metals 18 percent, and Alcan nine percent.

Any new capacity can take up to four years from construction to full production, and an estimated sustained price of 85 cents per pound is needed to justify new capacity, last seen in 1989, Oppenheimer said.
LME cash settled Wednesday at 68 cents a lb.

China was set to import more, while Eastern Europe would export less as domestic consumption rises. Net imports of the West were estimated at 2.1 million tonnes this year, falling to 1.75 million in 1997 and 1.6 million in 1998.
Oppenheimer expected cash aluminum prices to average 85 to 90 cents in 1997, and exceed an average of $1 a lb in 1998.
"Aluminum equities, in our opinion, should be represented in portfolios," Oppenheimer said. Alcoa, Reynolds Metals, Alcan and Alumax were all rated Buy.
